newsitem.title: USA: U.S. should focus more on emerging markets - Garten.
newsitem.headline: U.S. should focus more on emerging markets - Garten.

text.p: The U.S. must wake up to the importance of the big emerging markets or risk being left behind in the 21st century, Jeffrey Garten said.

"We need a sharp departure from our business-as-usual foreign policy approach, (which dictates) that most of our attention ought to be on Europe and Japan," Jeffrey Garten, dean of the Yale School of Management, told Reuters in an interview.
Garten, who served as U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade from 1993 to 1995, has identified 10 emerging countries which he believes will reshape the world in the next century.
In his first public splash since leaving the Clinton administration, Garten makes his case in a new book, "The Big Ten: The Big Emerging Markets and How They Will Change Our Lives."

Garten said that the 10 countries to watch are spread across the globe: Mexico, Brazil and Argentina in the Americas; China, India, Indonesia and South Korea in Asia; Poland and Turkey in Europe; and in Africa, South Africa.
"Most of them at one time or another were the centers of civilization in their regions, and they're coming back," Garten said. "We're not according them the right sort of respect."
Garten believes there is a dangerous vaccuum of leadership in Washington, and that the U.S. business community is hiding its collective head in the sand.

Despite ongoing charges of U.S. campaign irregularities and corporate welfare, Garten argues that the U.S. actually needs more, and not less, "commercial diplomacy" -- the intersection of foreign policy, government power and business deals.
"The heart of our foreign policy ought to be pursuing our commercial goals," he said. "Not just for commercial reasons, but because this is where influence is going to be."

Garten said it would be tragically misguided for the U.S. to remove China's most-favored nation (MFN) trade status. U.S. President Bill Clinton is expected to make a decision by June 3, after which Congress will deliberate.
Although both liberals and conservatives are turning up the heat on Clinton to cancel China's MFN, Garten said it is wrongheaded for the U.S. to link trade and human rights.

"I think it's going to be a real test for the administration to remain very tough, because unless we engage China economically, we will have no influence on China. That goes for these other (big emerging markets) too."
He said that unilateral trade bans by the U.S. actually create more problems than they solve.
"We may get some short-term moral satisfaction, but we hurt our firms, (and) we lose political influence."
Unlike the situation of just a few years ago, emerging markets today realize that there are many alternatives to trading with the U.S.
"There's nothing that we can sell the Chinese that they can't buy from Europe or Japan," Garten said.
Garten said that the first Clinton administration got off to an excellent start in reshaping foreign policy, but that the effort was derailed by the 1994 Congressional elections.

He said his book is not intended to be a harsh critique of Clinton. "I'm trying to -- with the freedom of not being in the administration -- say, 'You were right all along, keep it up, and don't get deflected.'"
